title: Position: Behavioral Systems Require Behavioral Tests
claim: Advancing behavioral evaluation requires three complementary priorities: tracing action sequences, varying environments systematically, and studying interacting adaptive agents.
layout: 3 side-by-side framed panels, left-to-right, black title bars
description: Three equal rounded-border panels, each with a black header bar and white serif title. Left, 'Chains of Actions': a state graph runs from a teal start node S1 to an orange end node St. A yellow-green path of actions a1, a2, ..., a(t-1) sits above a brown path of hidden intermediate states. Thin brown lines link the two paths, and a magnifying glass with a question mark suggests inferring the strategy. Center, 'Systematic Environments': a 2x4 grid of arched windows or doors in varied pastel colors and layouts, each with a different symbol such as a checkmark, arrow or dot. Right, 'Multi-agent Systems': six gray, tan and brown person icons joined by black arrows in a network. The eye goes first to the black titles, then to the colorful central grid.
caption: We propose three specific priority areas for advancing behavioral evaluation of AI systems: (left) recovering decision-making strategies from sequences of actions; (center) using environment variants to test causal influences on behavior; (right) analysis of emergent behavior in multi-agent systems where agents adapt to each other’s presence.
abstract: Artificial agentic systems increasingly operate as behavioral systems by interacting with dynamic environments, pursuing goals, and adapting over time. Yet, current evaluation methods largely focus on performance outcomes, not the underlying behavioral processes that produce them. This paper argues that AI agents must be evaluated like other behavioral systems: through systematic observation, perturbation, and interpretation of their actions. We draw on lessons from the behavioral sciences to motivate this position, and propose a research agenda focused on developing rigorous behavioral tests. These include methods for recovering decision strategies from action sequences, constructing environments that isolate behavioral differences, and probing emergent dynamics in multi-agent systems. Taken together, these directions offer a roadmap for developing a science of AI behavior.
